content: Matico, also known as spiked pepper, is a flowering plant belonging to the Piperaceae family. Its scientific name is Piper aduncum, and it is synonymous with Piper angustifolium, Piper celtidifolium, and Piper elongatum. The plant emits a characteristic peppery odor, which is common among many species in this family. The fruits of Matico are utilized as a condiment and are also employed to flavor cocoa. In some cases, it serves as a substitute for long pepper. In the Amazon Rainforest, indigenous tribes use Matico leaves for their antiseptic properties. In Peru, the plant has been traditionally used to stop hemorrhages and treat ulcers. In European medical practices, it has been applied in the treatment of diseases affecting the genital and urinary systems, often as an alternative to cubeb. Matico is a tropical, evergreen, shrubby tree that can grow to a height of 6 to 7 meters (20 to 23 feet). Its leaves are lance-shaped and measure between 12 to 20 centimeters (5 to 8 inches) in length. The plant is native to regions such as Southern Mexico, the Caribbean, and much of tropical South America. It is also cultivated in tropical Asia, Polynesia, and Melanesia, and can be found in areas like Florida, Hawaii, and Puerto Rico. However, in some countries, Matico is considered an invasive weed. In parts of New Guinea, despite its reputation for depleting soil moisture in areas where it is invasive, the wood of the plant is still utilized by local communities for various purposes, including as fuel and for constructing fence posts. According to legend, the plant was discovered by a wounded Spanish soldier named Matico. He reportedly learned from local tribes that applying the leaves to his wounds effectively stopped the bleeding. This led to the plant being referred to as Matico or soldier's herb. Matico was introduced into the field of medicine in the United States and Europe in 1839 by a Liverpool physician. It was used as a styptic and astringent for treating wounds.
